video_title: Do small residential batteries make sense?
gist: David Roberts presses Cole Ashman, ex-Tesla Powerwall/SPAN engineer and CEO of Pila Energy, on whether 1.6 kWh plug-in 'permissionless' home batteries make sense. Ashman argues that whole-home batteries have stalled below 1% of US homes because soft costs are over 50% of installed cost, and that drop-shipped, meshed LFP battery nodes can win the grid edge by killing deployment friction. He says utilities (e.g., in PJM, where transmission costs are set by five one-hour coincident peaks) now prefer predictable ~2 kW battery load reductions over thermostats and EV chargers. Roberts counters that per-kWh cost (~$930/kWh at $1,500) matches an installed Powerwall 3 and that residential time-of-use arbitrage is worth only ~$50–60/yr, leaving backup power and third-party financing as the real drivers.

insights.claim: Cole Ashman (Pila Energy CEO, ex-Tesla Powerwall) says that after a decade of deployment, fewer than 1% of US homes have any large whole-home battery from Tesla, Enphase, Franklin or others, which he blames on the installer-driven deployment model rather than on demand.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Residential storage penetration remains tiny; installer/permitting friction, not hardware, is the binding constraint on the addressable market.
insights.quote: there's still fewer than 1% of US homes that have any large whole home battery

insights.claim: Ashman says whole-home battery projects typically cost roughly $15,000 to $50,000 as electrician-installed, permitted upgrades, and that over 50% of a whole-home battery system's cost is not the hardware.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Falling cell prices alone will not make installed home storage cheap; the value pool lies in collapsing soft costs (installation, permits, truck rolls).
insights.quote: over 50% of the cost of a whole home battery system is is not the hardware

insights.claim: David Roberts calculates that Pila's $1,500, 1.6 kWh plug-in battery works out to about $930/kWh, roughly the same per-kWh cost as an installed Tesla Powerwall 3; Ashman concedes the per-unit energy cost is not lower, attributing parity to eliminating soft costs by design.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host) / Cole Ashman
insights.so_what: Plug-in batteries are not a cheaper $/kWh product today; their edge is deployment speed and reach (renters, condos), not unit energy cost.

insights.claim: Pila raised its plug-in battery price from $1,000 at March 2025 pre-orders to $1,500, which Ashman blames on supply chains strained by data-center demand making chips expensive, citing Apple's base MacBook moving from $1,299 to $1,499.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: AI data-center demand is spilling over into consumer-electronics and energy-hardware input costs, inflating BOMs across device categories.
insights.quote: Supply chain is CO level crazy right now

insights.claim: Ashman expects the cost of producing and delivering plug-in batteries to fall predictably through mass-manufacturing scale, unlike installer economics, permits and truck rolls, which have proven very hard to compress for whole-home systems.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Manufactured, drop-shipped storage should ride a learning curve that installed storage cannot, favoring hardware-scale plays over installer-heavy models.

insights.claim: Ashman argues the grid of the future will be balanced at its edges, and that the edge will be won by whoever kills deployment friction and so builds the largest coordinatable fleet.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Frames DER competition as a fleet-scale race; fleet size (not per-unit capability) may be the key metric for valuing distributed-storage platforms.
insights.quote: the grid edge is kind of one by friction reduction and speed of deployment

themes.theme: Who buys plug-in batteries and why

insights.claim: Pila's shipped customer base is 60% homeowners and 40% renters, roughly mirroring US housing stock, where about half of homes are renter/condo households that could not install a whole-home battery even if they wanted to.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Plug-in storage opens a large 'white space' segment (renters/condos) structurally excluded from the Powerwall-style market.

insights.claim: About 50% of Pila's customers are in California, Texas and the Northeast, where power prices are rising and outages are getting worse, though it ships to all 50 states and has a backlog larger than it can fulfill.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Demand for distributed storage concentrates where reliability is deteriorating and rates are rising — useful for sizing regional DER markets.

insights.claim: More than half of Pila customers order multiple units, and about one in five already own a whole-home battery and add Pila for extra capacity and appliance-level monitoring.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Plug-in batteries appear complementary rather than cannibalistic to Powerwall-type systems, suggesting layered demand for home storage.

insights.claim: Ashman says 80% of US households with rooftop solar do not have a battery, making no-contractor add-on batteries a large retrofit opportunity.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: The installed base of solar-only homes is a large, underpenetrated attach-rate market for storage retrofits.
insights.quote: 80% of households with solar on their roof don't have a battery today

insights.claim: Ashman says backup power, not bill savings, is what gets most consumers to buy a home battery, because higher bills are merely frustrating while blackouts are visceral; consumers already spend billions on generators, UPS units and portable systems.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Residential storage demand tracks outage frequency more than rate spreads; grid reliability deterioration is the key demand catalyst.
insights.quote: a higher bill is is frustrating, but a blackout's visceral

insights.claim: Pila's mapping analysis finds about one in three US counties have experienced both higher power prices and worse outages over the last five years, a share Ashman says is increasing.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: A broad and growing geographic base of households faces the price-plus-reliability squeeze that drives backup and storage purchases.
insights.quote: It's like one in three counties in the US have had both higher prices and worse outages in the last 5 years.

insights.claim: Ashman notes Tesla Powerwall and Enphase batteries hold roughly 85% market share despite costing about 2x the cheaper option, arguing reliability and quality, not the cheapest box, win in home energy.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Premium brands command pricing power in home storage; cheap portable-battery entrants may struggle to take share on price alone.
insights.quote: Tesla Power Wall and Nphase batteries have something like 85% market share

insights.claim: Ashman says only about 10% of homes buy pull-start generators or have backup generators today, a backup niche that plug-in storage must move beyond to reach mass market.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Backup alone caps the market at ~10% of homes; mass adoption depends on subsidized or infrastructure-financed models.

insights.claim: David Roberts estimates that with a ~20-cent peak/off-peak spread and ~10 W standby draw, a 1.6 kWh plug-in battery saves only about $50–60 a year on time-of-use rates; Ashman agrees that framing such batteries as 'money printers' is disingenuous and says there is no nationwide payback number.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host) / Cole Ashman
insights.so_what: Standalone residential arbitrage cannot justify small batteries; investors should treat consumer payback claims skeptically and look for third-party value capture.
insights.quote: framing these things as money printers is maybe a bit disingenuous

insights.claim: Roberts notes that residential bill savings from small batteries largely require time-of-use rates, which many utilities' customers (e.g., most Con Edison customers) are not on; Ashman adds that demand-charge management offers lucrative savings for commercial users and some residential customers in Arizona.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host) / Cole Ashman
insights.so_what: Rate design determines storage economics; commercial demand-charge customers are the stronger near-term savings market than residential.

insights.claim: Ashman claims Pila's residential IRR/payback is equal to or better than a standard whole-home battery system, while acknowledging that savings are often a post-hoc rationalization behind backup-driven purchases.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Home storage in general is a weak pure-financial investment for households, reinforcing the need for utility or financier subsidies.

themes.theme: Utilities, PJM peaks and battery-based demand response

insights.claim: Ashman says that in PJM, customer cost-to-serve is increasingly driven by transmission costs set by five coincident peaks per year, each about an hour long, and that New Jersey utilities evaluating Pila are targeting about a 2 kW load reduction per residential customer.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Coincident-peak transmission charges create a concrete, monetizable target for short-duration, behind-the-meter storage in PJM.

insights.claim: Ashman argues batteries beat smart thermostats for peak reduction because thermostat control increases load before and after the event (precooling and recovery) and requires occupant compromise, while batteries are predictable and invisible to the occupant.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Challenges thermostat-led DR programs; battery-based DR may take share of utility demand-response budgets.

insights.claim: Ashman cites studies showing that an EV charger with 7–8 kW of nominal capacity delivers an average load reduction of only about 400 W once you account for whether it is online, the car is plugged in, and charging coincides with the event.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Managed EV charging is far less reliable a grid resource than its nameplate suggests — a haircut for VPP valuations built on EV flexibility.
insights.quote: the actual kind of average load reduction from an EV charger is something like 400 watts

insights.claim: Ashman says utilities are increasingly focused on solving peak problems with batteries after years of 'toiling' in an IoT smart-device promised land that never materialized, and that drop-shipped batteries avoid installers and PUC-approval complexity.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Signals a shift in utility DR procurement toward storage-based resources, positive for distributed-battery vendors.

insights.claim: Ashman says grid needs are increasingly power problems lasting one to two hours, so Pila designs 'big engine, small tank' batteries, whereas Tesla's Powerwall was built as 'medium engine, big tank' to shift solar about 12 hours into the night.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Short-duration, high-power storage is optimized for coincident-peak and transmission-cost reduction rather than daily solar shifting.

insights.claim: Holy Cross Energy, a Colorado co-op facing wildfire risk and public safety power shutoffs, is piloting Pila batteries that it pays for and deploys in the first phase, enrolling them in VPP/demand-response programs across residential, single-family, multifamily and business customers.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Wildfire-driven shutoffs are spreading beyond California (to Colorado), creating utility-funded resilience-plus-DR demand for distributed storage.

insights.claim: Pila is working with Brooklyn Solar Works and other solar installers to sell plug-in, AC-coupled batteries to solar-only customers in New York City who could not get whole-home batteries for structural, code or cost reasons.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Plug-in storage can open code-constrained urban markets like NYC where installed batteries have struggled.

insights.claim: Pila has an innovation partnership with PG&E, with batteries installed at PG&E's San Ramon 'electrified home of the future' facility, and Ashman says utilities value customer-opted-in appliance data because they lack visibility into the last mile of the distribution grid.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Granular behind-the-meter data is becoming a monetizable asset as distribution planning grows in importance.

insights.claim: Ashman claims the lifetime value of distributed batteries is several multiples of their build cost, which could let partners finance them like infrastructure and effectively give them away to customers for free.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: If true, distributed storage is an infrastructure-finance asset class — watch for utility, ESCO and third-party-owned battery programs.
insights.quote: these batteries are actually worth multiples of the cost it takes to build them

insights.claim: Pila is working with David Energy, utilities that own or discount batteries, large solar companies, VPP operators and ESCOs, and expects the next wave of partners to include commercial real estate owners and insurance providers.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Insurers and landlords as storage buyers would broaden the capital pool for behind-the-meter batteries beyond energy incumbents.

insights.claim: Ashman expects the future mix to shift away from customers paying full retail toward rebates, discounts and utility-funded deployment in exchange for customers opting into a few hours of grid events per year, while still allowing upfront purchase with no subscription fee.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Business model is migrating from consumer hardware sales toward utility-paid capacity — revenue quality depends on utility program economics.

insights.claim: Ashman argues consumer smart-home technologies such as smart doorbells tap out at 10–20% early-adopter penetration, whereas infrastructure like utility smart meters reaches ~80%, so distributed batteries must be deployed as infrastructure to reach scale.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Useful adoption-ceiling heuristic: consumer-pull energy devices plateau around 10–20%; utility-pushed infrastructure models reach far higher penetration.
insights.quote: You you kind of tap out at 10 to 20% of early adopters pretty quickly.

insights.claim: Host David Roberts identifies a recurring theme across his recent interviews: clean energy is migrating from a consumer product to infrastructure.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Suggests value in clean energy may shift from consumer brands toward utilities, financiers and infrastructure-style platforms.

insights.claim: Ashman attributes lithium-ion fires such as New York City's e-bike fires to low-cost, high-power-density NMC/NCA packs that are often value-engineered and abused, whereas Pila and most home batteries use heavier but significantly safer lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: LFP has become the default for stationary home storage on safety grounds, supporting LFP cell suppliers.

insights.claim: Ashman says plug-in batteries occupy a regulatory gray area in New York City — Pila is not listed as an energy storage system because current product standards are not written for it — and Pila is engaging the FDNY and building department while its batteries carry cellular radios for monitoring.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Reclassification as ESS is a regulatory risk for plug-in battery makers in dense cities, though Ashman calls it paperwork risk only.

insights.claim: Ashman predicts that within three to five years US households will be able to feed power back into a standard outlet in a controlled, safe way, driven by UL and NEC code-making processes rather than sweeping legislation, citing Germany's millions of balcony-solar homes as precedent.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Outlet-level export would unlock plug-in solar and battery export in the US, expanding the plug-in DER market; watch UL/NEC rule changes.
insights.quote: in 3 to 5 years we will absolutely see here in this country in the US ability to feed back into an outlet

insights.claim: Ashman notes there are roughly 50 bills in 35 states on balcony/plug-in solar, but argues real progress comes through 'very boring' UL and NEC code-panel discussions.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Legislative momentum for plug-in solar is broad; codes and standards bodies are the real gating catalyst to monitor.

insights.claim: Ashman says Pila is chemistry-agnostic and not in the battery chemistry game, though he finds sodium-ion and other chemistries interesting; the company's differentiation is controls and coordination.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Value in distributed storage is shifting to software/controls, making cells a commodity input.

themes.theme: Embedded storage and the coordination layer

insights.claim: Asked whether batteries built into stoves, Carrier air conditioners, appliances and buildings will squeeze out standalone batteries, Ashman agrees storage will be embedded everywhere within about 10 years and the standalone 'battery' category will become less visible.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Standalone consumer batteries may be a transitional category; long-term value accrues to appliance makers integrating storage and to the coordination software layer.
insights.quote: I share that conviction. That will be the future in 10 years.

insights.claim: Ashman compares plug-in batteries today to the Roku/Fire Stick stage of smart TVs — an add-on bridge before capability is built in — and says the hard problem and Pila's focus is coordinating many storage devices to behave as one system that grids can count on.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Framework for DER investing: add-on hardware is a bridge; the durable moat is the coordination/software layer that aggregates embedded devices.
insights.quote: in this moment we are at the the Roku the Fire Stick stage of smart TVs

insights.claim: Ashman says that while working on Tesla Powerwall, analysis found 20–40% of systems disconnected from home Wi-Fi within six months because customers changed passwords or routers, costing Tesla significantly in maintenance and support — which is why Pila uses a local mesh network plus cellular backhaul.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Connectivity loss is a hidden cost and reliability risk for Wi-Fi-dependent VPP fleets; dedicated connectivity improves dispatchable-fleet reliability.
insights.quote: within 6 months, something like 20 to 40% of the Power Wall systems would disconnect from home Wi-Fi

insights.claim: Pila says its batteries can mesh up to 64 units in a home, and hundreds or thousands in commercial multi-tenant buildings, functioning as a distributed 'Megapack' on the urban grid.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Aggregated small batteries in commercial buildings could compete with front-of-meter urban storage for distribution-grid services.

insights.claim: Ashman argues appliance-level batteries can stretch limited capacity by modulating power using internal temperature data — treating a refrigerator or HVAC-cooled home as a thermal battery — something a single meter-level battery cannot do.
insights.speaker: Cole Ashman, Pila Energy
insights.so_what: Load-adjacent sensing and control can extract more flexibility per kWh, raising the effective value of small batteries.
